salsigne.title: At Salsigne, following the structures that channel fluids
salsigne.lead: Around the former Salsigne mine, this field report examines how tectonic structures may have influenced the movement and trapping of hydrothermal fluids associated with mineralisation.

sections.title: Two outcrops around Salsigne
paragraphs: The study compares two sites in the Montagne Noire: an outcrop west of Villardonnel and another north of Limousis. Located on either side of the mining area, they offer two views of the regional structural setting.
The aim is not only to describe the ore, but to place field observations within the architecture of the rock units, faults and shear zones.

sections.title: Field-scale clues
paragraphs: At Villardonnel, the schists contain quartz veins associated with the foliation and fractures that cut across it. The report distinguishes several generations of structures and silicification.

At Limousis, a fault and cataclastic zone are observed at the contact between different formations. Oxidation traces are described near the surface. These clues prompt a discussion of past fluid flow, but do not by themselves establish its source.

sections.title: An interpretation that remains open
paragraphs: The comparison suggests that some faults, shear zones and lithological boundaries may have acted as pathways or traps for mineralising fluids.

The report also highlights an important limitation: the observations do not identify the source of the fluids with certainty. This structural interpretation needs to be tested against further geological and metallogenic evidence.

salsigne.sourceNote: Summary based on an MSc field report (2024–2025).
references: Chardon, D., Aretz, M. & Roques, D. (2020). Reappraisal of Variscan tectonics in the southern French Massif Central. Tectonophysics, 787.
Lescuyer, J.-L. (2005). Salsigne — example of a late Variscan gold deposit, Southern French Massif Central.

coiron.title: Reading a dyke in the Coiron volcanic landscape
coiron.lead: A dyke is a sheet-like intrusion that cuts across its host rocks. At Coiron, field observation offers a starting point for examining its geometry and asking how it relates to the surrounding rocks.

sections.title: From landscape to outcrop
paragraphs: These photographs bring together wide views and close details of a volcanic outcrop. They document a field observation of a dyke made during an MSc internship focused on the Coiron volcanic system.
The first step is to examine the contact: where does the intrusion meet its host rock, what geometry does it form at outcrop scale, and which neighbouring structures should be mapped?

sections.title: Document before interpreting
paragraphs: A photograph helps preserve a field site, but it cannot replace field measurements. Orientation, thickness, contact relationships and links to fractures must be recorded to move from an image to a structural interpretation.
These images are field notes, not proof on their own of the dyke’s age, composition or role in the evolution of the massif.
